html:
The Brouwer Route was the sea route used by Dutch ships from the Cape of Good Hope to Java from the 1610s. Instead of sailing north along Africa and across the Indian Ocean with the monsoons, ships ran south from the Cape into the Roaring Forties and rode the strong westerly winds east, then turned north for Java.

Hendrik Brouwer of the Dutch East India Company first sailed it in 1611. It cut the voyage from about a year to around six months, with less disease, and in 1617 the company made it compulsory. The Cape became the halfway stop; see Dutch settle the Cape.

Sailors could not measure longitude well, so they often did not know when to turn north. Some ships went too far and hit the unknown west coast of Australia. In 1616 Dirk Hartog landed there and left an inscribed pewter plate, and others charted parts of the coast they called New Holland. Some were wrecked, among them the Batavia in 1629, whose survivors suffered a notorious mutiny and massacre. In this way the route led Europeans to Australia.
